title: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course
summary: The examples on this site run in your browser, but from chapter 4 on you will build real Windows programs, step through them in a debugger and read their memory. That takes **Visual Studio** on your own PC. This lesson installs it with the right parts, creates a console project, and sets the options the course assumes.
markdown:
## Why Visual Studio Visual Studio is Microsoft's development environment for Windows. It brings together the three tools this course leans on most: - the **MSVC compiler and linker**, which produce the same kind of code as the Windows programs you will study, - the **Windows SDK**, the headers and libraries for the Windows API, - the **Visual Studio debugger**, which can pause a program, show its memory and registers, and step through its machine code. The **Community** edition is free for individual learners. It runs on Windows 10 and 11. The examples on this site use the same compiler, so code that runs here behaves the same way there. > [!note] Visual Studio, not Visual Studio Code > Visual Studio Code is a separate, lighter editor. It can be set up for C++, but its debugger and project system are not what this course describes. Install **Visual Studio** (the purple icon). ## Installing 1. Download the **Visual Studio Community** installer from Microsoft's website: `visualstudio.microsoft.com`. 2. Run it. When it asks which **workloads** to install, tick **Desktop development with C++**. 3. On the right, under **Installation details**, make sure these are ticked. Most are on by default: - MSVC v143 (or newer) x64/x86 build tools - Windows 11 SDK (the newest listed; it also builds programs for Windows 10) - C++ AddressSanitizer (used in chapter 2) - C++ CMake tools for Windows (optional) 4. Press **Install**. It needs several gigabytes and some time. Later chapters add more: chapter 16 installs the **Windows Driver Kit**, and says exactly which version to match. Nothing else is needed now. ## Creating a project 1. Start Visual Studio and choose **Create a new project**. 2. Pick **Console App** with the C++ tag. Not "Empty Project" and not a C# one. 3. Name it, for example `chapter01`, choose a folder, and tick **Place solution and project in the same directory** to keep the folders simple. 4. Press **Create**. Visual Studio opens `chapter01.cpp` with a "Hello World" program in it. Press **Ctrl+F5** (Start Without Debugging). A console window opens and shows the output, and stays open until you press a key. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["Solution (.sln)
a set of projects"] --> P["Project (.vcxproj)
one program or library"] P --> F1["chapter01.cpp"] P --> F2["other .cpp and .h files"] P --> O["x64\Debug\chapter01.exe
the build output"] ``` A **project** builds one program or library. A **solution** groups projects that belong together; chapter 4 uses this to build a game and a DLL side by side. ## Settings the course assumes Open the project's properties: right-click the project in **Solution Explorer** and choose **Properties**. At the top, set **Configuration** to **All Configurations** and **Platform** to **x64**, so the changes apply to both Debug and Release builds. | Where | Setting | Value | Why | |---|---|---|---| | General | C++ Language Standard | ISO C++20 Standard (`/std:c++20`) or newer | The course uses `std::format`, `std::span` and other C++20 features | | C/C++ → General | Warning Level | Level 4 (`/W4`) | More warnings catch more mistakes | | C/C++ → General | Treat Warnings As Errors | Yes (`/WX`), optional | Stops warnings from piling up unread | | Advanced | Character Set | Use Unicode Character Set | The default; chapter 5 explains what it changes | And in the toolbar at the top of the window, make sure the platform box says **x64**, not x86. Everything in this course assumes 64-bit programs: 8-byte pointers, the x64 registers, the x64 calling convention. ## Debug and Release The toolbar's configuration box switches between two ways of building the same code. | | Debug | Release | |---|---|---| | Optimisation | Off | On (`/O2`) | | Code matches the source line by line | Yes | Not closely: code is merged, reordered or removed | | Extra checks | Uninitialised stack memory filled with `0xCC`, heap checks, iterator checks | None | | Speed | Slow | Fast | | Use it for | Writing and debugging | Measuring performance, and shipping | Most of this course uses **Debug**. Chapter 4 compares the two in detail, and chapter 7 reads optimised Release code on purpose. > [!tip] The `0xCC` pattern > In a Debug build, uninitialised local variables are filled with the byte `0xCC`. If a variable shows up as `-858993460` (which is `0xCCCCCCCC`) in the debugger, you have read it before giving it a value. You will meet this pattern in the next lesson. ## Where the output goes After a build, the program is in a folder named after the platform and configuration: ``` chapter01\ chapter01.cpp chapter01.vcxproj x64\ Debug\ chapter01.exe the program chapter01.pdb its debug symbols Release\ chapter01.exe ``` You can run the `.exe` from there by double-clicking it, but a console program closes its window as soon as it finishes. Run it from a terminal instead: open **Tools → Command Line → Developer PowerShell**, then: ```powershell cd x64\Debug .\chapter01.exe ``` The **Developer PowerShell** also has the compiler on its path, so you can try the build stages from lesson 1.04 by hand: ```powershell cl /EHsc /std:c++20 /c main.cpp # compile only: makes main.obj cl /EHsc /std:c++20 /FA main.cpp # compile and link, and also write main.asm dumpbin /disasm main.obj # show the machine code inside the object file ``` ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Building for x86 > A 32-bit build has 4-byte pointers and a different calling convention, and nothing in chapters 6, 7 or 9 will match. Check the platform box says x64. > [!warning] Changing settings for one configuration only > If Debug builds work and Release builds fail with odd errors, a setting was probably changed with only Debug selected. Use **All Configurations** when setting project-wide options. > [!warning] Picking the wrong project template > "Console App" under C++ is the one. Templates for C#, or a "Windows Desktop Application", start from different code. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? Which workload do you need in the Visual Studio installer for this course? - .NET desktop development + Desktop development with C++ - Game development with Unity > It brings the MSVC compiler, the Windows SDK and the C++ debugger. ? A variable shows as `-858993460` in the debugger. What does that suggest? + It was read before being given a value, in a Debug build - It holds a very large negative score - The debugger is broken > -858993460 is `0xCCCCCCCC`, the pattern Debug builds use to fill uninitialised stack memory. ? Why should the platform be set to x64? - x86 programs cannot run on Windows 11 + The course's material on pointers, registers and calling conventions describes 64-bit programs - Visual Studio Community only supports x64 > Both build fine, but a 32-bit program has different pointer sizes, registers and calling conventions from everything the course explains. ```
ideas:
- Create the `chapter01` project and run the default program with **Ctrl+F5**.
- Paste in the `GetSystemInfo` example from the last lesson and run it. You should see the same numbers as on this site.
- Switch to **Release**, build, and compare the size of `x64\Debug\chapter01.exe` with `x64\Release\chapter01.exe` in File Explorer.
- Open the Developer PowerShell and compile a file with `cl /FA`. Open the `.asm` file it writes and find your `main`.

cards.q: What is the difference between a project and a solution?
cards.a: A project builds one program or library from its source files. A solution is a container for one or more related projects.

cards.q: Name two ways a Debug build differs from a Release build.
cards.a: Debug has optimisation turned off, so the code follows the source line by line, and adds checks such as filling uninitialised memory with `0xCC`. Release is optimised: faster, but harder to follow in a debugger.

cards.q: Where does Visual Studio put the program it builds?
cards.a: In a folder named after the platform and configuration, such as `x64\Debug\`, next to its `.pdb` debug symbols.
